title: A Busy Product Page
statement: A shop's product page gets 5,000 reads per second at peak. The database can serve about 1,000 reads per second and cannot be upgraded this quarter. Product details change a few times a day, and a price that is up to 60 seconds old is acceptable. Which read path fits best?
examples: Most reads ask for a few hundred popular products
A price change must reach users within 60 seconds
constraints: The database stays at about 1,000 reads per second
Data may be up to 60 seconds old

approaches.name: Read every request from the database and add more servers in front of it
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.time: All 5,000 reads per second reach the database
approaches.why: More servers only send more reads to the same database, which can serve about 1,000 per second. The bottleneck stays.

approaches.name: Cache-aside with a 60-second TTL, and delete the cache entry on every change
approaches.label: best
approaches.time: Hits ≈1 ms; with a 90% hit rate, 500 database reads per second
approaches.why: Most reads become hits, so the database stays within its limit. Deleting on change makes new prices visible at once, and the TTL keeps any missed delete within the 60-second rule.

approaches.name: Cache-aside with a 60-second TTL and no delete on change
approaches.label: valid
approaches.time: Same hit rate and database load
approaches.why: This meets both requirements, because a changed price is shown within 60 seconds. It is simpler, but users see old prices for up to a minute after every change, which deleting on change avoids.

approaches.name: Cache-aside with no TTL and no delete
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.space: Memory grows with every product read
approaches.why: A changed price would never reach the cache, which breaks the 60-second rule.

title: Showing an Account Balance
statement: A banking app shows a user's account balance. Right after a transfer, the balance on screen must be exact. Balance reads are about 300 per second, and the database serves them easily. The profile name and settings shown next to the balance change rarely. What should the team cache?
examples: A user sends money and opens the balance screen one second later
constraints: The balance must be exact right after a change
The database has plenty of capacity for 300 reads per second

approaches.name: Cache the balance with a 5-minute TTL
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: A user could see the old balance for up to 5 minutes after a transfer, which breaks the first requirement.

approaches.name: Read the balance from the database; cache only the rarely changing profile name and settings
approaches.hint: Cache what can be a little old
approaches.label: best
approaches.time: Balance read from the database, settings ≈1 ms
approaches.why: The balance is always exact, and the database has capacity for it. Caching the rarely changing parts still saves work where slightly old data is harmless.

approaches.name: Do not cache anything on this screen
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: This meets both requirements, because the database handles 300 reads per second easily. It gives up a small saving on the settings that could safely be cached.

title: Product Images Around the World
statement: A shop with its servers in Virginia, USA, sells worldwide. Product photos are 200 to 500 KB each, the same for every user, and change only when a seller uploads a new photo. Users in Asia wait several seconds for the images. How should the images be served?
examples: A user in Hanoi opens a product page with 8 photos
constraints: A new photo must replace the old one for all users within an hour
Photos are the same for every user

approaches.name: Move the photos to a faster server in Virginia
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.time: Each photo still crosses the ocean
approaches.why: The slow part is the distance to Asia, not the server's speed, so a faster server in Virginia does not remove the long round trips.

approaches.name: Serve photos through a CDN with a TTL of one hour
approaches.label: valid
approaches.time: Nearby edge when it has a copy
approaches.why: This meets both requirements: photos come from a nearby edge, and a new photo appears within an hour. Edges fetch every photo again each hour, even unchanged ones, which costs more traffic to the origin.

approaches.name: Serve photos through a CDN with a long TTL, and give every new photo a new file name
approaches.hint: A new name means a new copy
approaches.label: best
approaches.time: Nearby edge for almost every photo
approaches.why: Unchanged photos stay at the edges for a long time, and a new upload gets a new name, so the page links to the new file at once. This meets the one-hour rule with fewer requests to the origin.

approaches.name: Keep the photos in the Virginia server's memory
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: An origin cache saves disk reads in Virginia, but users in Asia still wait for every round trip across the ocean.
